around.headline: Arms supplier tied to Bengaluru chemist's murder nabbed after police encounter
around.summary: The suspected illegal-arms maker who attacked officers with a sword and chilli powder during a midnight raid — and was shot in the leg — has now been linked to the recent Bengaluru chemist murder case, per today's reports. If you're near the raid's locality, expect continued police activity as this week's wider crackdown (nearly 500 rowdy-sheeters screened) continues.
around.source: The Indian Express, Deccan Herald, The Times of India

around.headline: Eid Milad clash: nine arrested, three FIRs filed in Basavanagudi
around.summary: Police have arrested nine people and filed three FIRs over Wednesday's Eid Milad procession clash in Basavanagudi — up from six arrests reported yesterday, per today's report. If you live or commute through that area, expect a continued heavier police presence this weekend.

around.headline: Auto, taxi unions give 15-day deadline over bike-taxi apps, threaten bandh
around.summary: Bengaluru's auto and taxi unions have set a 15-day deadline demanding action against bike-taxi apps and say they'll call a citywide bandh if it isn't met, per today's report. If you rely on autos or cabs for your commute, keep an eye on this over the next two weeks and have a backup plan ready.
around.source: The Times of India, The Hindu, Deccan Herald

around.headline: Namma Metro Purple Line to run at reduced speed for six weeks; Green Line hit by glitch
around.summary: The Purple Line's older trains will run at a speed-restricted 40 kmph between Benniganahalli and Baiyappanahalli for six weeks during a mid-life overhaul, while BMRCL separately confirmed a technical glitch disrupted Green Line services today, per today's reports. Budget extra travel time on both lines if they're on your route.

around.headline: 300 drug batches — from paracetamol to IV fluids — found substandard in Karnataka
around.summary: A state drug-testing report flagged 300 medicine batches, ranging from common paracetamol to hospital IV fluids, as substandard, per today's report. Buy medicines from licensed pharmacies and check packaging and batch details look intact before use, especially for anything hospital-supplied.

around.headline: Nepal flash-flood crisis deepens as fresh glacial lakes form at avalanche source
around.summary: Fresh glacial lakes have formed at the source of Nepal's ice-rock avalanche, raising fears of further flooding, even as the state death toll climbs; Karnataka's CM office says 13 state residents remain stranded and 4 NRI pilgrims are still missing, per today's reports. If you have relatives travelling in the region, stay in touch and watch for state helpline updates.

street_smart.title: A caller claiming to be from your bank's fraud department says unusual activity was just flagged on your account, and reads out your card's last four digits to sound legitimate. He says an OTP is about to hit your phone to 'cancel the suspicious transaction' — read it out so he can stop it. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: No single incident in today's feeds fits the choice-based trap format cleanly (today's Bengaluru stories — an arms-supplier arrest tied to a chemist's murder, updated Eid Milad clash arrests, a Metro Purple Line speed restriction, and 300 substandard drug batches found statewide — don't lend themselves to a 'best move' scenario), so this rotates in from the evergreen list: OTP/social-engineering scams. This specific mechanism last appeared as the street-smart scenario on 2026-08-04 (a SIR-registration-themed OTP scam), outside the three-week window; every other evergreen topic (digital-arrest scams and phone snatching on 08-28, two-wheeler theft on 08-27, auto/cab overcharging and UPI fraud on 08-26, rental traps as recently as 08-22, credit-card skimming on 08-16, loan-app harassment on 08-15, consumer court on 08-18, and fake job offers on 08-09) has run more recently.
street_smart.situation: A few seconds later, your phone actually does buzz with an SMS from your bank's real sender ID, containing a genuine 6-digit OTP.

choices.text: Hang up immediately, and call your bank back yourself using the number printed on your card or its official app — never a number the caller gave you.
choices.feedback: Correct. No bank, card network, or telecom employee ever needs your OTP to 'stop' or 'verify' a transaction — the OTP exists precisely so only you can authorize one, and reading it out hands that authorization to whoever asked. Hanging up and calling the number on your own card confirms whether the alert was even real, on a line you know is genuine.

choices.text: Read out the OTP so he can 'cancel' the suspicious transaction, since he already knew your card's last four digits so he must be legitimate.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Scammers often already have partial card or account details from a prior data leak or a fake online order — knowing your last four digits proves nothing about who's actually calling. The moment you read the OTP out, you're not stopping a transaction, you're authorizing one for the scammer.

choices.text: Don't read the OTP out loud, but stay on the line and follow his instructions to open your banking app and 'verify' your account there instead.
choices.feedback: Not reading the OTP is a good instinct, but staying on the call and letting him direct you through your banking app still hands over control — a scammer can talk you through screen-sharing or a fund transfer just as easily as an OTP. Hang up and act only through channels you initiate yourself.

choices.text: Ask him detailed questions to verify he's real — your registered address, past transactions — before deciding whether to share the OTP.
choices.feedback: Trying to verify the caller sounds cautious, but it keeps you engaged with the scam's script instead of ending it, and a well-prepared scammer with leaked data can often answer basic questions too. The only real verification is calling the bank back yourself on their official number.

takeaways: No bank, telecom company, or card network will ever ask you to read out an OTP over a call — it's designed to be entered only by you, never spoken to anyone.
A caller already having some of your details (last four digits, address) only proves data leaked somewhere — it doesn't verify who's calling you now.
When in doubt, hang up and call back using the number on your card or the bank's official app — never a number the caller gives you or that shows on your screen.

quiz.question: Why was Bengaluru's first 'peptide party' in Koramangala cancelled, per today's reports?
options: The Food Safety and Drug Administration sought regulatory details
The organiser cancelled due to low ticket sales
quiz.why: Karnataka's FSDA issued a notice seeking regulatory details before the event, prompting its cancellation just a day before it was due to happen.

quiz.question: Namma Metro's Purple Line will run at what reduced speed for six weeks starting soon, per today's report?
quiz.why: The speed restriction, between Benniganahalli and Baiyappanahalli, is part of a mid-life overhaul of the line's older trains — 15 years after they entered service.

quiz.question: Jio Platforms received Sebi approval this week for what is set to become India's biggest-ever what?
quiz.why: The approved IPO is reported at roughly Rs 37,700 crore, which would make it the largest public listing in Indian stock market history.

quiz.question: What is the official currency of Nepal, the country at the centre of this week's deadly flash floods?
quiz.why: The Nepalese Rupee is pegged to the Indian Rupee at a fixed rate of 1.6 NPR to 1 INR.

quiz.question: What is the SI unit of electric current?
quiz.why: The ampere is named after French physicist André-Marie Ampère, a pioneer of classical electromagnetism.
